title: Explain the cause of lunar phases

AST101-lecture-order.brief: The Moon is always half lit: the Sun lights whichever half faces it. As the Moon orbits Earth over about 29.5 days, we see different amounts of that lit half, and those amounts are the phases. Earth's shadow plays no part, except during a lunar eclipse. Quick check: when the Moon is full, where is the Sun?
AST101-lecture-order.standard:
Hold on to one sentence: **the Moon is always half lit**. The Sun lights the half facing it, all the time. The phase you see is how much of that lit half faces Earth, and that depends on the angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth.

Picture the lamp-and-ball model from lecture. A bare lamp is the Sun, a ball at arm's length is the Moon, your head is Earth. Ball toward the lamp: you see its dark side, a new moon. A quarter turn later, half the face is lit: first quarter. Ball opposite the lamp: the whole lit face points at you, a full moon. The cycle takes about 29.5 days.

Notice what never happens: your head's shadow never touches the ball, unless the ball is exactly behind your head. That is a lunar eclipse, the only time Earth's shadow matters.

Your turn: a thin crescent hangs low in the west just after sunset. Where is the Sun, and why can't Earth's shadow be making that crescent?
AST101-lecture-order.thorough:
Most people think Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases. It is a good wrong answer, and it is worth replacing, because the right idea also explains rise times and eclipses.

**The core idea.** The Moon makes no light; it reflects sunlight. At every moment the Sun lights exactly half of it. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different fractions of that lit half. The fraction depends only on the angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth.

**The model.** In the lamp-and-ball activity, the lamp is the Sun, the ball is the Moon and your head is Earth. Turn slowly in a circle:

- Ball between you and the lamp: dark side toward you, **new moon**.
- A quarter of the way around: half the face lit, **first quarter**.
- Ball opposite the lamp: whole lit face toward you, **full moon**.
- Three quarters around: the other half lit, **third quarter**.

From new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days.

**A worked example.** Because the phase is an angle, it tells you the clock. A full moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises as the Sun sets and sets as the Sun rises. A first quarter Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun, so it rises around noon and is highest at sunset. That is why you can see the Moon in the afternoon.

**Two pitfalls.** First, the shadow idea fails a simple test: Earth's shadow points away from the Sun, but a crescent Moon appears close to the Sun in the sky. The shadow reaches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, at full moon. Second, "quarter" means a quarter of the way around the orbit, not a quarter lit; a quarter Moon looks half lit.

Now you try. Sketch the top-down view: Sun far to the left, Earth in the middle, the Moon a quarter of the way around. Which half of the Moon is lit, which half faces Earth, and what phase do you see?

AST101-big-ideas-first.brief: One big idea runs through this course: what we see depends on where things sit relative to the Sun. For the Moon, that means it is always half lit, and the phase is how much of the lit half faces us, set by the Sun-Earth-Moon angle. No shadow needed. Which phase do you see when the Moon is opposite the Sun?
AST101-big-ideas-first.standard:
Start with the big idea of AST 101: **geometry decides what we see**. Where the Sun, Earth and Moon sit relative to each other explains the phases now, and it will explain eclipses and the seasons next.

For the phases, the geometry is simple. The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, about once every 29.5 days, the angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth changes, and so does how much of the lit half faces us.

- Moon toward the Sun: we see the dark side, a **new moon**.
- Moon 90 degrees from the Sun: half the face lit, a **quarter** phase.
- Moon opposite the Sun: the whole lit side, a **full moon**.

Earth's shadow is not part of it. The shadow points away from the Sun and touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, at full moon.

Try the big idea on a new case: if you see a half-lit Moon high in the south at sunset, how far around its orbit from the Sun is it?
AST101-big-ideas-first.thorough:
The most useful idea in AST 101 is a geometric one: **what we see depends on where things sit relative to the Sun**. Daily motion, the phases, eclipses and the seasons all follow from it. The phases are the cleanest place to see it work.

**The geometry.** The Moon shines by reflected sunlight, and the Sun always lights exactly half of it. The Moon orbits Earth about once every 29.5 days (new moon to new moon), so the angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth keeps changing. The phase is simply how much of the lit half faces us at that angle.

- 0 degrees from the Sun: **new moon**, dark side toward us.
- 90 degrees: **first quarter**, half the face lit.
- 180 degrees: **full moon**, the lit side toward us.
- 270 degrees: **third quarter**, the other half lit.

**Why this is a big idea.** The same angle also tells time. A full moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises at sunset. A first quarter Moon rises around noon and is highest at sunset. And the angle sets up eclipses: a solar eclipse needs the Moon at 0 degrees (new), a lunar eclipse at 180 (full), plus the Moon crossing Earth's orbital plane. One picture, many predictions.

**The misconception to drop.** Earth's shadow does not cause the phases. The shadow points away from the Sun, but a thin crescent appears right next to the Sun in the evening sky. The shadow only reaches the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

**Check yourself.** Build the lamp-and-ball model: a lamp, a ball at arm's length, your head as Earth. Turn slowly and watch the lit part change while your head's shadow stays off the ball.

Now predict before you check: if the Moon is at third quarter, about what time does it rise, and where is it at sunrise?
